## Dynamic Programming, You mean Programming
- What even *is* dynamic programming? When I was first introduced to the concept, it just felt like regular programming and honestly, it kinda is. The name sounds like a buzzword someone invented to make loops sound impressive.
- The point of dynamic programming is a key one in computer science: remove redundant computations. When you solve a problem recursively
you usually end up doing the same subproblem many times over. The classic example here is the fibonacci sequence notice how `fib(2)` gets recomputed over and over:

```
                     fib(5)
                   /        \
              fib(4)        fib(3)
             /     \        /     \
        fib(3)   fib(2)  fib(2)  fib(1)
        /    \
    fib(2)  fib(1)      ← fib(2) shows up 3 times, and it only gets worse
```

- Dynamic programming ends up producing really elegant, neat solutions. They have this quality where you look at the finished answer and go "yeah,
I got it, that's simple" but do not be lulled into that trap. When you're facing the problem cold, there are some genuine logical leaps to make solutioning *forward*
that feel obvious only when you're verifying in arrears.
- There are a few common patterns that these dynamic programming problems tend to follow, and we'll demystify a couple of them here.

## DP Approaches
- How do we avoid recomputation then? There are two main approaches a top down and a bottom up approach.
  - The top down approach caches your computations allowing you to do a look up instead
of recomputing, this is called memoization.
  - The bottom up approach builds up from a base case, this is called tabulation.
- My CS Masters class, shout out OMSCS, focuses on tabulation, so this article only dives into that specifically.

## Patterns
A handful of shapes cover most DP problems. The hard part isn't the code, it's
spotting *which shape you're in*.

| Pattern | State | Smells like |
|---|---|---|
| **Ending at `i`** | best solution that *ends at* element `i` | LIS, max subarray |
| **Prefix** | best over the *first `i`* items | climbing stairs, house robber |
| **Two prefixes** | `T[i][j]` over first `i` of A, first `j` of B | LCS, edit distance |
| **Interval** | `T[i][j]` over the *subarray* `i..j`, split at `k` | matrix chain |
| **Capacity** | `T[i][w]` = first `i` items within budget `w` | knapsack |

## Example 1 — Hotel Stops (1D)

You're going on a road trip. The road starts at mile 0, and there are `n` hotels
at mileposts $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$. You can stop at any hotel, but you *must*
end the trip at the last one. Ideally you'd drive exactly 200 miles a day, so a
day covering $x$ miles costs a penalty of $(200 - x)^2$ — the further from 200,
the worse it stings. Minimize the total penalty.

```
   start                                          must
   ● ────── ● ────── ● ────── ● ────── ● ────── ●  end
   0        50       125      200      300      500
            a₁       a₂       a₃       a₄       a₅
```

My first instinct was to be greedy — just drive as close to 200 miles as I can each
day. Greedy locks you into a good-looking first leg that strands you later. This is an
**ending-at-`i`** problem: fill the table with the best cost to *end a day* at each
hotel. Since the trip must finish at the last hotel `n`, the answer we want is `T[n]`.

The trick to DP is usually to think about the last decision. To get to some hotel $a_i$
you had to come from some *earlier* hotel $a_j$, or you drove
there straight from the start. If it came from $a_j$, that last leg is $a_i - a_j$
miles costing $(200 - (a_i - a_j))^2$, plus the best cost of getting to $a_j$,
which is already in the table we are building: $T[j]$. If it came from the start, the leg is just
$a_i$ miles, costing $(200 - a_i)^2$.

> **State** &nbsp; `T[i]` = min total penalty for a trip ending at hotel $a_i$
> **Base** &nbsp; `T[1] = (200 - a_1)^2` — the first hotel can only be reached from the start
> **Recurrence** &nbsp; $T[i] = \min\Big( \underbrace{(200 - a_i)^2}_{\text{from the start}},\ \ \min_{1 \le j < i}\big( \underbrace{T[j] + (200 - (a_i - a_j))^2}_{\text{via hotel } a_j} \big) \Big)$
> **Order** &nbsp; fill `i` left to right; answer at `T[n]` (the trip must end at the last hotel)
> **Runtime** &nbsp; `O(n²)` — `n` cells, each scanning up to `n` earlier hotels


Filling the table:

```
   i        1      2      3      4      5
   aᵢ      50    125    200    300    500
   T[i]  22500   5625      0   6250   6250
                                       ▲ answer
```

`T[5] = 6250`. The optimal stops are
**0 → 125 → 300 → 500**.


## Example 2 — Unique Paths (2D grid)

This is a fun one because it's so obvious *after the fact*, but when I first looked
at it and thought about the brute force solution, my mind had a hard time keeping
track of all the potential paths.

> A robot sits in the top-left corner of an `m × n` grid. It can only move **right**
> or **down**, one cell at a time, and wants to reach the bottom-right corner. How
> many **distinct paths** can it take?

```
   ● ─▶─ □ ─▶─ □
   │     │     │      ● start   (top-left)
   ▼     ▼     ▼      ★ goal    (bottom-right)
   □ ─▶─ □ ─▶─ □      moves: right or down only
   │     │     │
   ▼     ▼     ▼
   □ ─▶─ □ ─▶─ ★
```

Unlike the last example where we could use a 1-D table to build our solution, this one naturally gives way to a 2-D table to match the grid.

Last decision again: to *arrive* at cell `(i, j)`, I either came from exactly the cell **above** `(i-1, j)` or the cell to the **left**
`(i, j-1)`. So the number of ways to reach `(i, j)` is just the sum of the ways to
reach those two.

> **State** &nbsp; `T[i][j]` = number of distinct paths from the start to cell `(i, j)`
> **Base** &nbsp; the entire top row and left column are `1`
> **Recurrence** &nbsp; `T[i][j] = T[i-1][j] + T[i][j-1]`
> **Order** &nbsp; fill row by row; answer at `T[m][n]`
> **Runtime** &nbsp; `O(m·n)` — one grid, constant work per cell


Filling a 3×3 grid, each inner cell = the cell above plus the cell to its left:

```
   1   1   1
   1   2   3
   1   3   6   ← answer
```

## Example 3 — Knapsack, without repetition (capacity)

You're loading up a daypack for a hike. There are `n` snacks — a granola bar, a
suspiciously heavy apple, a single glorious chocolate croissant — each with a
**weight** `wᵢ` and a **yum** value `vᵢ`, and your pack holds at most `W` grams.
You've only got one of each snack, so you either toss it in or leave it behind. No,
you cannot bring three croissants. Maximize the total yumminess you carry.

The tells: you're choosing a **subset** of items under a **budget** (`W`). That's
the **capacity** pattern — a 2D table indexed by *which items you've considered* and
*how much room is left*.

Last decision: look at item `i`. Two choices:

- **Leave it.** Your best is whatever you'd get from the first `i-1` items with the
  same room: `T[i-1][w]`.
- **Take it.** You gain `vᵢ`, but it eats `wᵢ` of your capacity, so the rest comes
  from the first `i-1` items with `w - wᵢ` room left: `vᵢ + T[i-1][w - wᵢ]`.

Take the better of the two.

> **State** &nbsp; `T[i][w]` = max value using the first `i` items with capacity `w`
> **Base** &nbsp; `T[0][w] = 0` (no items), `T[i][0] = 0` (no room)
> **Recurrence** &nbsp; `T[i][w] = max( T[i-1][w],  vᵢ + T[i-1][w - wᵢ] )` &nbsp; *(second term only if `wᵢ ≤ w`)*
> **Order** &nbsp; fill row by row; answer at `T[n][W]`
> **Runtime** &nbsp; `O(n·W)`

::: {.callout-important}
## The one detail that makes it "without repetition"
Both branches look at row **`i-1`**, never row `i`. That's what forbids reuse: once
you've decided about item `i`, you drop to the previous row so you can't grab it
again.
:::

With snacks `A` = granola `(w2, v3)`, `B` = apple `(w3, v4)`, `C` = croissant `(w4, v5)` and a pack of `W = 5`:

```
              w=0   1    2    3    4    5
   (none)      0    0    0    0    0    0
   + A(2,3)    0    0    3    3    3    3
   + B(3,4)    0    0    3    4    4    7
   + C(4,5)    0    0    3    4    5    7   ← answer
```

`T[3][5] = 7`, achieved by packing `A` and `B` (weights `2 + 3 = 5`, yum
`3 + 4 = 7`). The croissant is the tastiest single snack but doesn't fit alongside
anything good; tragic, but the table doesn't care about your feelings.


## Wrap Up
- So it turns out dynamic programming really *is* just programming you've just stopped redoing your own homework. 
- The two ways to avoid recomputation are **memoization** (top-down, cache as you recurse) and **tabulation** (bottom-up, fill from a base case). Same answer, different direction.
- The actual hard part was **spotting the shape**. We saw a few different ones:
  - **ending-at-`i`** (hotels), where every earlier stop competes to be your predecessor
  - **2D grid** (unique paths), where a cell is just the two cells feeding into it
  - **capacity** (knapsack), where one index — `i-1` vs `i` — is the whole difference between "one croissant" and "infinite croissants"
- The closest thing to a single trick is this: **think about the last decision**. Assume every smaller subproblem is already solved, ask what the final choice could have been, and take the best of your options. Solutioning forward is hard; verifying in arrears is easy*ier*. DP just lets you build the whole thing out of the easy direction.
